pl-l3d13c1-d1e117.summary: States that Christ as man received the fullness of grace from his very conception, to whom the Spirit was given not by measure (Jn 3:34) and in whom the fullness of divinity dwells bodily (Col 2:9).
claims: Christ as man had the fullness of grace from conception.

pl-l3d13c1-d1e126.summary: Cites Augustine, Ad Dardanum: the fullness of divinity dwells in Christ so that he is full of all grace, not so in the saints. As in our body sense is in each member but not as much as in the head, which has sight, hearing, smell, taste, and touch while the others have only touch, so the fullness of divinity dwells in Christ the head, and in the saints, given the Spirit by measure, there is as it were only touch. They receive from his fullness not by essence but by likeness, a like grace, not the same. So the child was full of wisdom and grace from conception.
claims: Christ is the head with all grace; the saints have grace by measure.
The saints receive a grace like Christ's, not the same grace.

pl-l3d13c1-d1e148.summary: Cites Jer 31:22, 'a woman shall encompass a man', as fitting, since in the Virgin's womb there was a perfect man, not only in soul and flesh but in the wisdom and grace with which he was full.
claims: Christ was a perfect man in the womb, full of wisdom and grace.

pl-l3d13c1-d1e154.summary: Raises an objection from Lk 2:52: Jesus advanced in wisdom, age, and grace before God and men; if he advanced, he does not seem to have had fullness of grace without measure from conception.
claims: Objection: Christ's advancing in wisdom implies he lacked fullness.

pl-l3d13c1-d1e163.summary: Answers that as man he received from conception such fullness of wisdom and grace that God could not give him more; yet he truly advanced in wisdom and grace, not in himself but in others, who advanced from his wisdom and grace as he revealed its gifts more and more with age.
claims: God could not give Christ more wisdom and grace.
Christ advanced in wisdom in others, not in himself.

pl-l3d13c1-d1e166.summary: Cites Gregory: he advanced in wisdom according to human nature, not by becoming wiser over time, since he was full of wisdom from conception, but by gradually showing it to others; he advanced in age from infancy to youth; he advanced in grace by revealing, not acquiring, it. 'Before God and men' because the more he revealed his gifts, the more he stirred people to praise God, advancing for the Father's praise and men's salvation. So he advanced in others, as a church ruler advances in his charge when others advance by his effort.
claims: Christ advanced in wisdom by revealing it, not by acquiring it.
Christ's progress was in others.

pl-l3d13c1-d1e187.summary: Notes that elsewhere it is written that he advanced according to human sense, as he advanced in human age.
claims: Some texts say Christ advanced in human sense.

pl-l3d13c1-d1e191.summary: Cites Ambrose, De Spiritu sancto III: God assumed the perfection of human nature, took human sense though not puffed up by carnal sense; by human sense his soul was troubled, he hungered, prayed, and advanced. Progress in age and wisdom is human: if he advanced in human age, he advanced in human wisdom. Which sense advanced? If human, it was assumed; if divine, it would be changeable, which the divine is not. So the human sense advanced, and he took a human sense.
claims: Christ assumed a human sense, which advanced.
The divine cannot advance or change.

pl-l3d13c1-d1e206.summary: Continues Ambrose: God's power cannot be strengthened nor God grow nor God's wisdom be filled; what was filled was our wisdom. Isaiah says the child would not know father or mother (Is 8:4): God's wisdom is not deceived about the future, but infancy, lacking knowledge, is ignorant of what it has not learned. Attributing two principal senses or two wisdoms does not divide Christ, any more than adoring his divinity and flesh, or saying he took a rational soul, divides him: the Word was not in place of a rational soul in his flesh, but he took a rational soul and flesh like ours and was perfect man.
claims: What advanced in Christ was human wisdom.
Two wisdoms do not divide Christ.
The Word did not replace a rational soul in Christ.

pl-l3d13c1-d1e224.summary: Comments that Ambrose's words must be read with pious care, since partly they enlighten and partly, misunderstood, they feed error. They plainly teach two principal senses or two wisdoms in Christ, without dividing his person: according to his two natures he has two wisdoms, one uncreated and begotten, which he is, the other not begotten but created and given by grace, as Isaiah foretells (Is 11:2). As God he is wise, good, and just by the natural wisdom, goodness, and justice that he is; his soul is wise, good, and just by gifts of grace that it is not. One person is wise by eternal wisdom as God and by gratuitous wisdom as man.
claims: Christ has two wisdoms, uncreated and created.
His soul is wise by a gift of grace distinct from itself.
The one person is wise by both human and divine sense.

pl-l3d13c1-d1e230.summary: Asks how Ambrose's statement that the human sense advanced should be understood, since he seems to say that Christ advanced in human understanding, that his infancy lacked knowledge, and that he did not know his father and mother, which the Church does not accept and the earlier authorities do not allow.
claims: Christ's real ignorance in infancy is not accepted by the Church.

pl-l3d13c1-d1e239.summary: Answers that it can soundly be read as referring to appearance to men and display of his understanding: his human sense advanced in display and in others' opinion. Likewise he is said not to have known father and mother in infancy because he behaved as if he lacked knowledge.
claims: Christ's human progress was in display and others' opinion.
Christ only behaved as if ignorant in infancy.

pl-l3d13c1.summary: Teaches that Christ as man received the fullness of grace from conception, the Spirit not given by measure and the fullness of divinity dwelling in him bodily. As the head has all the senses and the members only touch, so Christ has all grace and the saints receive from his fullness by likeness, not by the same essence. The objection from Lk 2:52 (Jesus advanced in wisdom and grace) is answered: he had from conception such fullness that God could not give more, and advanced in others by revealing it gradually, as Gregory says. Ambrose's teaching that he advanced in human sense raises the issue of two wisdoms: an uncreated wisdom, which he is, and a created wisdom given by grace to his soul, in one person. Ambrose's words about progress and childhood ignorance are read as referring to appearance and others' opinion.
claims: Christ as man had the fullness of grace and wisdom from conception.
The saints receive from Christ's fullness a like grace, not the same.
Christ advanced in wisdom and grace in others, not in himself.
Christ has two wisdoms, uncreated and created, in one person.
Christ's apparent progress and childhood ignorance refer to appearance.
